what_it_does: After a quantum computer runs a circuit, reading out the final state of each qubit is imperfect — the measurement process itself introduces errors. A technique called readout error mitigation corrects these errors mathematically by applying a matrix that maps noisy measurement outcomes back to the ideal ones, but as the number of qubits grows the matrix grows exponentially, making computation and memory demands impractical. DyREM exploits the fact that in any real quantum computation only a small fraction of all possible bit-string outcomes actually occur (the probability distribution is 'sparse' — most entries are near zero). By detecting which outcomes are non-negligible and dynamically building a much smaller mitigation matrix on the fly using only those entries (via tensor products, a way to assemble the full matrix from per-qubit pieces), an embedded hardware accelerator keeps the computation manageable even at larger qubit counts.
